As some people here will know, my belief is that the recent idea that "autoformalization is solved" is currently wildly over-stated. What is currently happening is that people are choosing targets which are accessible to current autoformalization tools and solving them. On the other hand my team in London are looking at modern papers in the top journals and are finding that we cannot even _state_ the main theorems in many cases, and furthermore that the project to _state_ the theorem can be a highly nontrivial challenge.

With this in mind, I present v0.1 v0.2v0.3 (incorporating suggestions of S. Gouezel) of the Jacobian Challenge. The code below has not been reviewed and I am not an expert in the differential geometry part of the library so I reserve the right to edit the challenge to make it more idiomatic.

The current version of the challenge will always be available at https://tinyurl.com/JacobianChallenge or https://gist.github.com/kbuzzard/778bc714030b3e974ab5f4038783d1a9 .

import Mathlib -- compiles with commit 8e3c989104daaa052921bf43de9eef0e1ac9fbf5 (15th April 2026)

/-

# Jacobians

An AI challenge to make an API for Jacobians, by Kevin Buzzard. v0.2.

## Main missing definitions

* `genus` -- genus of a compact Riemann surface
* `Jacobian` -- the Jacobian of a compact Riemann surface
* `Jacobian.ofCurve` -- the Abel-Jacobi map from a compact Riemann surface to its Jacobian
* `ContMDiff.degree` -- the degree of a holomorphic map between compact Riemann surfaces.
    Equal to 0 if the map is constant, otherwise equal to the usual degree.
* `Jacobian.pushforward` -- the pushforward map on Jacobians induced by a holomorphic map between
  compact Riemann surfaces.
* `Jacobian.pullback` -- the pullback map on Jacobians induced by a holomorphic map between
  compact Riemann surfaces.

## Main missing theorems

* `genus_eq_zero_iff_homeo` -- a compact Riemann surface has genus 0 iff it is homeomorphic to
     the sphere
* `ofCurve_inj` -- the Abel-Jacobi map is injective iff the genus is positive
* `Jacobian.ofCurve_contMDiff` -- the Abel-Jacobi map is holomorphic
* `Jacobian.pushforward_contMDiff` -- the pushforward map is holomorphic
* `Jacobian.pullback_contMDiff` -- the pullback map is holomorphic
* `pushforward_pullback` -- pullback then pushforward is multiplication by degree

## Changelog

* v0.2: `Type*` not `Type u`; use `𝓘(ℂ)` instead of `modelWithCornersSelf ℂ ℂ`; docstrings
  and comments
* v0.1: initial public release
-/

open scoped ContDiff -- for ω notation

open scoped Manifold -- for 𝓘 notation

/-- The genus of a compact Riemann surface. -/
def genus (X : Type*) [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X] [CompactSpace X] [ConnectedSpace X]
  [Nonempty X] [ChartedSpace ℂ X] [IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ) ω X] : ℕ := sorry

-- let X be a compact Riemann surface
variable {X : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X] [CompactSpace X] [ConnectedSpace X]
  [ChartedSpace ℂ X] [IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ) ω X]

-- this proof avoids the hack answer `∀ X, genus X = 0`
lemma genus_eq_zero_iff_homeo :
    genus X = 0 ↔ Nonempty (X ≃ₜ (Metric.sphere (0 : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)) 1)) :=
  sorry

universe u in
-- data
/-- The Jacobian of a compact Riemann surface. -/
def Jacobian (X : Type u) [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X] [CompactSpace X] [ConnectedSpace X]
  [Nonempty X] [ChartedSpace ℂ X] [IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ) ω X] : Type u := sorry

namespace Jacobian

-- data
/-- The Jacobian of a compact Riemann surface is naturally an additive commutative group. -/
instance : AddCommGroup (Jacobian X) := sorry

-- data
/-- The Jacobian of a compact Riemann surface is naturally a topological space. -/
instance : TopologicalSpace (Jacobian X) := sorry

-- Prop
instance : T2Space (Jacobian X) := sorry

-- Prop
instance : CompactSpace (Jacobian X) := sorry

-- data
/-- The Jacobian of a compact Riemann surface is a complex manifold, of dimension
equal to the genus of the surface. -/
instance : ChartedSpace (Fin (genus X) → ℂ) (Jacobian X) := sorry

-- Prop
instance : IsManifold (modelWithCornersSelf ℂ (Fin (genus X) → ℂ)) ω (Jacobian X) := sorry

-- Prop
instance : LieAddGroup (modelWithCornersSelf ℂ (Fin (genus X) → ℂ)) ω (Jacobian X) := sorry

/-- The Abel-Jacobi map from a compact Riemann surface to its Jacobian. -/
def ofCurve (P : X) : X → Jacobian X := sorry

lemma ofCurve_contMDiff (P : X) : ContMDiff 𝓘(ℂ)
    (modelWithCornersSelf ℂ (Fin (genus X) → ℂ)) ω (ofCurve P) := sorry

lemma ofCurve_self (P : X) : ofCurve P P = 0 := sorry

-- this is the lemma which stops the hack answer "J(X)=0 for all X"
lemma ofCurve_inj (P : X) (h : 0 < genus X) : Function.Injective (ofCurve P) := sorry

variable {Y : Type*} [TopologicalSpace Y] [T2Space Y] [CompactSpace Y] [ConnectedSpace Y]
  [Nonempty Y] [ChartedSpace ℂ Y] [IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ) ω Y]

variable (f : X → Y) (hf : ContMDiff 𝓘(ℂ) 𝓘(ℂ) ω f)

/-- The pushforward map between Jacobians associated to a map of the underlying curves. -/
def pushforward (f : X → Y)
    (hf : ContMDiff 𝓘(ℂ) 𝓘(ℂ) ω f) :
    Jacobian X →ₜ+ Jacobian Y := sorry

-- pushforward is holomorphic
theorem pushforward_contMDiff :
  ContMDiff (modelWithCornersSelf ℂ (Fin (genus X) → ℂ))
  (modelWithCornersSelf ℂ (Fin (genus Y) → ℂ)) ω (pushforward f hf) := sorry

-- functoriality
lemma pushforward_id_apply (P : Jacobian X) : pushforward id contMDiff_id P = P := sorry

variable {Z : Type*} [TopologicalSpace Z] [T2Space Z] [CompactSpace Z] [ConnectedSpace Z]
  [Nonempty Z] [ChartedSpace ℂ Z] [IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ) ω Z]

variable (g : Y → Z) (hg : ContMDiff 𝓘(ℂ) 𝓘(ℂ) ω g)

-- functoriality
lemma pushforward_comp_apply (P : Jacobian X) :
    pushforward (g ∘ f) (hg.comp hf) P = pushforward g hg (pushforward f hf P) :=
  sorry

/-- Pullback map between Jacobians associated to a map of the underlying curves.
Equal to the zero map if the map on curves is constant. -/
def pullback (f : X → Y)
    (hf : ContMDiff 𝓘(ℂ) 𝓘(ℂ) ω f) :
    Jacobian Y →ₜ+ Jacobian X := sorry

-- pullback is holomorphic
theorem pullback_contMDiff :
    ContMDiff (modelWithCornersSelf ℂ (Fin (genus Y) → ℂ))
      (modelWithCornersSelf ℂ (Fin (genus X) → ℂ)) ω (pullback f hf) := sorry

-- functoriality
lemma pullback_id_apply (P : Jacobian X) : pullback id contMDiff_id P = P := sorry

-- functoriality
lemma pullback_comp_apply (P : Jacobian Z) :
    pullback (g.comp f) (hg.comp hf) P = pullback f hf (pullback g hg P) := sorry

/-- The degree of a holomorphic map between compact Riemann surfaces. Equal to zero
for constant maps, otherwise equal to the usual degree. -/
def _root_.ContMDiff.degree
    (hf : ContMDiff 𝓘(ℂ) 𝓘(ℂ) ω f) : ℕ :=
  sorry

lemma pushforward_pullback (P : Jacobian Y) :
  pushforward f hf (pullback f hf P) = (ContMDiff.degree f hf) • P := sorry

end Jacobian

As it's plain to see, this is a Lean file with a bunch of sorrys in. However in contrast to many formalization challenges, some of the sorries are defs. Aha, you might think! There could be a trick here: define all of the objects to be the wrong things, like the trivial group or whatever, and then prove all of the theorems with these wrong definitions and we have a classic AI hack which solves the problem in an incorrect way.

But what I've tried to do in this experiment is to write a sufficiently large amount of API for these definitions to ensure that it is impossible to give incorrect definitions whilst simultaneously filling in all of the sorrys.

All the mathematical ideas needed to fill in these sorries are classical, probably everything was known in the 19th century. Jacobian.ofCurve is the Abel-Jacobi map; Abel died in 1829 and Jacobi in 1851. All the LLMs will be able to write as detailed a plan as you like for filling in these sorries. My claim is that filling in these sorries in Lean, which will require differential geometry which can simultaneously be described as "completely standard masters-level material" and "a highly nontrivial extension of the material we have in Mathlib" will be an extremely difficult problem for current autoformalization systems. I would love to be proved wrong.

Note that autoformalization of FLT will involve having to solve challenges which are 100x as difficult as this. I hope that this challenge is able to put things into some kind of focus. I still think that autoformalization of FLT is a long way off and this challenge represents what I perceive as one of the bottlenecks.

Those people in this community who think that autoformalization will soon solve everything -- this challenge is to solve something which humans did nearly 200 years ago. I hope this puts things into focus.

Maybe? Let me say something about what I did rather than what I could have done.

Let X be a compact Riemann surface of actual genus 2 or more. It's not homeomorphic to the sphere so a sorry in the file forces X to have AI genus at least 1. Now to fill in other sorries we have to come up with an injective holomorphic map from X to a compact connected Lie group of AI dimension at least 1 and it seemed to me that already asking this is asking a nontrivial thing, whether it's the Jacobian or not; in fact I suspect that the Jacobian is the easiest example!

The reason I think that this is a hard challenge is that all definitions of Jacobian that I know involve quotienting a manifold by a discrete group, which isn't in mathlib as far as I know. The one where you use XgX^gXg by the symmetric group involves a delicate local analysis when points coincide and the one where you quotient out the dual of the holomorphic 1-forms by the first homology will involve integrating differentials around loops which we don't have either, at least in this generality (as far as I know).

Once you show me that you can do this, we can then talk about the 2020s."

I want to ask the question: can AI be useful for mathlib? Right now there is a lot of anti-AI sentiment, especially amongst mathlib reviewers who are being faced with a deluge of ok-but-needs-work PRs from AIs and the reviewers have finally thrown up their hands and said "this is pointless, I don't want to explain to an AI why their PR is mediocre because they will not learn so I am not motivated to put in the effort". On the other hand a human formalization of Jacobians will take months. If an AI can formalize a nice definition and then prove enough theorems about it to convince people that the definition is correct and usable then perhaps a human can then PR just the definition and a super-basic API to mathlib, perhaps all the AI proofs end up in merely-true or whatever, but mathlib can then state the theorem about Jacobians and we have made progress.

Just a quick spot check, here is what Claude asks me back in plan mode:

> How should we construct the Jacobian, given Mathlib's current state?

1. Period lattice: ℂ^g / Λ
     Define J(X) = ℂ^g / Λ where Λ is the period lattice from integrating a basis of holomorphic 1-forms over H₁(X,ℤ). Most classical; requires 1-forms, integration, and H₁.
2. Pic⁰(X) via divisors
     Define J(X) = degree-0 divisors modulo principal divisors. Algebraic; needs divisors and meromorphic functions on a Riemann surface.
3. Cohomological: H¹(X,𝒪)/H¹(X,ℤ)
     Define J(X) as a quotient of sheaf cohomology groups. Cleanest theoretically; needs sheaf cohomology for complex manifolds in Mathlib.
4. Defer decision to Phase B
     Decide after we've surveyed what Mathlib actually supports at the pinned commit. (Recommended — the right choice depends on what exists.)

These look vaguely reasonable from my surface (har) understanding, but I don't understand it enough to make the call. Not sure if making this choice correctly is part (or even the core) of the challenge, but it is definitely very consequential.

If I push Claude to make the call (with recommendation not to limit itself on what is in or not in mathlib, but what should be long-term the best definition for mathlib), the recommendation is

  Revised recommendation: still Option 1, but the canonical basis-free form.
  Jacobian X  :=  (H⁰(X, Ω¹_X))ᵛ  ⧸  (image of H₁(X, ℤ) under the period pairing)

Or maybe this is complete non-sense that is made to look plausible (something AI is very good at)

I did the same curiosity check, for me after thinking for 10 minutes it wrote me a whole plan, but then when I asked it how long it would take it to complete it it told me "Honestly — I can't do it." and that it'd be a multi-month project. Of course in none of its planning did I see it go off and look for existing resources which actually had proofs or definitions of anything Kevin mentioned so it didn't even give itself a shot at being successful there, it's possible with more prodding than my prompt it would be more (over)confident.

Apocryphally, some of the folks that have had success on erdos problems were also sharing they have to “confidence boost” their agents with prompts because they are unwilling to take tasks that have low chance of success (I know how ridiculous all this sounds :))

Aside: this behaviour would make sense for humans: getting praising for results/skill (instead of effort) makes humans stick more to tasks they can surely do (as this way, they match the expectation put on them).

All of these strategies are viable but a lot of work will be needed to push any of them through.

For the first one, one piece of hard work is writing down the map from Lambda to C^g (integrating differential forms on a manifold). For the second one, the hard part is putting a complex manifold structure on the group (will need Riemann-Roch and more). For the third one (and maybe for all of them) one issue will be proving that the spaces are finite-dimensional (maybe needs Serre duality).

Of course the real challenge would be to prove that the Jacobian is all three of these definitions; this is what mathlib would really want. But it is hard work to even write down some of these definitions.
For having recently ppl played a bit with autoformalization I think that what really helps is a human who know well the library (and the math!) and can at least suggest which path to follow.
For those classical problems the LLM is able to write a plan, but as noted there are several possibilities and the AI needs some guidance. In my experience this can speed up the process a lot.

totally, i think that's the elephant in the room for autoformalization. At least to me it is clear that, math _and_ lean expert with AI tooling would produce the by far the best results. The human needs to do high-level design and steering the AI can do the chorish details. The problem is AI companies are not incentivized to talk about that combo because 1) you can't train the hill-climbing well with a slow human in the loop 2) you can't sell the final product with a human in the loop. But my guess is all the successful "fully autonomous" results have had a secret very knowledgable human steering behind the scenes, but I don't see that as a failure, as long as they are honest about it.

Also the whole world has very few of the prerequisite math and lean experts, so their time is highly contested to be experimenting with AI powered workflows. So as an approximation you get people like me that are neither lean or math experts trying to steer the autoformalization poorly. Maybe that is of some value, maybe not, the only downside is maybe polluting the zulip conversations.

Well I simply don't know the most likely route to formalisation success here. All the suggestions above seem reasonable to me but I think we're missing a bunch of API and intermediate definitions needed to pull any of them off. Again let me stress that this is completely standard 19th century mathematics and would not be out of place in a masters or even advanced undergraduate course. It's easy to extol the virtues of what we have but the Annals formalisation project has been a harsh reminder of what we are missing and how hard it will be to get it. import Mathlib -- compiles with commit b80f227 (20th April 2026)

/-
# Jacobians in algebraic geometry

An AI challenge to construct the Jacobian of an algebraic curve, inspired by Kevin Buzzard's
version for Riemann surfaces.

Current version: v0.1

## Main missing definitions

In the following, by a smooth curve we mean a geometrically irreducible, smooth scheme of relative
dimension one over a field.

* `AlgebraicGeometry.genus` -- genus of a proper, smooth curve
* `AlgebraicGeometry.Jacobian` -- the Jacobian of a proper, smooth curve
* `AlgebraicGeometry.Jacobian.ofCurve` -- the Abel-Jacobi map from a proper smooth curve to its
  Jacobian

## Main missing theorems

* `AlgebraicGeometry.Jacobian.smoothOfRelativeDimension_genus` -- The Jacobian of a proper, smooth
  curve `C` is smooth of relative dimension `g`, where `g` is the genus of `C`.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.Jacobian.exists_unique_ofCurve_comp` -- the universal property of the Jacobian
  of a proper, smooth curve
-/

set_option autoImplicit false

universe u

open CategoryTheory Limits MonoidalCategory CartesianMonoidalCategory MonObj

namespace AlgebraicGeometry

variable {k : Type u} [Field k] (C : Over (Spec (.of k)))
  -- smooth curve
  [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom]
  -- proper
  [IsProper C.hom]
  -- geometrically irreducible
  [GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom]

-- data
/-- The genus of a smooth proper curve. -/
def genus (C : Over (Spec (.of k))) [IsProper C.hom] [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom]
    [GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom] : ℕ :=
  sorry

-- data
/-- The Jacobian of a smooth, proper curve over a field `k`. -/
def Jacobian (C : Over (Spec (.of k))) [IsProper C.hom] [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom]
    [GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom] : Over (Spec (.of k)) :=
  sorry

namespace Jacobian

/-! ## The Jacobian of `C` is an abelian variety. -/

-- data
/-- The group scheme structure on the Jacobian of the curve `C`. -/
instance : GrpObj (Jacobian C) :=
  sorry

/-- The Jacobian of `C` is smooth of relative dimension `g` over `k`, where `g` is the
genus of `C`. -/
instance smoothOfRelativeDimension_genus : SmoothOfRelativeDimension (genus C) (Jacobian C).hom :=
  sorry

/-- The Jacobian of `C` is proper over `k`. -/
instance : IsProper (Jacobian C).hom :=
  sorry

/-- The Jacobian of `C` is geometrically irreducible over `k`. -/
instance : GeometricallyIrreducible (Jacobian C).hom :=
  sorry

variable {C} in
-- data
/-- The Abel-Jacobi map from a smooth, proper curve to its Jacobian associated
to a `k`-rational point of `C`. -/
def ofCurve (P : 𝟙_ (Over (Spec (.of k))) ⟶ C) : C ⟶ Jacobian C :=
  sorry

/-- The Abel-Jacobi map sends the `k`-rational point `P` to `0`, where `0` (denoted by `η` below) is
the neutral element of the group scheme `Jacobian C`. -/
lemma comp_ofCurve (P : 𝟙_ (Over (Spec (.of k))) ⟶ C) :
    P ≫ ofCurve P = η[Jacobian C] :=
  sorry

/--
The universal property of the Jacobian variety: For any abelian variety `A`,
any morphism `f : C ⟶ A` such that `f(P) = 0` factors uniquely through the
Jacobian of `C`.
In other words, `Jacobian C` is the Albanese variety of `C`.
-/
theorem exists_unique_ofCurve_comp (P : 𝟙_ (Over (Spec (.of k))) ⟶ C)
    {A : Over (Spec (.of k))} [Smooth A.hom] [IsProper A.hom] [GrpObj A]
    [GeometricallyIrreducible A.hom] (f : C ⟶ A) (hf : P ≫ f = η[A]) :
    ∃! (g : Jacobian C ⟶ A), f = ofCurve P ≫ g :=
  sorry

end AlgebraicGeometry.Jacobian

Some notes:

  • Instead of asking for pushforward and pullback maps, I put the universal property of the Albanese instead.
  • This is in many ways the wrong generality, for example Spec(k)\mathrm{Spec}(k)Spec(k) should be replaced by a suitable base scheme S, but maybe a bit of flexibility is good and that way it is closer to the differential geometry version.

I agree with Kevin Buzzard's emphasis on formalizing definitions as a crucial challenge. As I read the discussion here, though, I feel that there are a couple of distinct sub-issues that are perhaps not being clearly distinguished.

Catchy names can sometimes be helpful. Let me define the Mind-Reading Problem as the problem of ensuring that a formal definition correctly captures what it is supposed to capture. This is what I was trying to get at with my example of an excellent doohickey versus a quasi-excellent special doohickey. I write a conventional mathematical text about doohickeys, proving that they are excellent. An AI, or another human for that matter, comes along and writes some code with a proof assistant. On the surface, the formal code defines doohickeys and excellence and correctly proves that all doohickeys are excellent. However, when I look carefully at the code, I see that what the code calls a doohickey is what I would call a special doohickey, and what the code calls excellence is what I would call quasi-excellence. There is nothing formally wrong with the proof, but what it actually establishes is the weaker result that all special doohickeys are quasi-excellent, not the stronger result that all doohickeys are excellent (as I would understand those terms). The AI (or other human) has failed to read my mind.

I've chosen the term "mind-reading" carefully, to emphasize that this is not a purely technical issue that can be solved just by developing a more powerful machine. Those who have read Quine's discussion of "gavagai" or Kripke's Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language will know that our apparent ability to read each other's minds is much more subtle than it appears at first glance. But even if you think that Quine and Kripke push the point too far, there remains a concrete practical issue here that cannot be breezily waved away by appealing to mere improvements in technology: how can we be sure that a formal definition correctly captures the concept that the human mathematical community intends?

Mind-reading aside, there's a second important concern that Kevin has raised concerning definitions. I can't think of quite as catchy a name, but let's call it the Iceberg Problem. The issue here is that what superficially looks like a simple definition cannot be formalized without first formalizing a large amount of prerequisites that lie hidden beneath the surface. Now, unlike the Mind-Reading Problem, the Iceberg Problem can be at least partially addressed by "mere" improvements in technology, just as the problem of autoformalizing very long proofs can be partially addressed by mere improvements in technology. However, the Iceberg Problem is intertwined with the Mind-Reading Problem. Trying to formalize a definition of an advanced mathematical concept will likely involve not just one instance of mind-reading, but long chains of mind-reading along the way, as other definitions pour out of Pandora's Box, demanding to be formalized as well. This is one reason why autoformalizing definitions is a distinct problem from autoformalizing proofs of theorems whose statements are known to be correct.

Following Tim's notation, Here is a concrete example of the Iceberg problem. I would love to be able to state Langlands' conjectures in Lean. These are conjectures relating Galois representations to automorphic representations. Galois representations -- we have essentially everything in mathlib! Automophic representations -- we do not have this definition. These are fundamental mathematical objects -- there are foundational problems in number theory which cannot be stated without them. There is at least one Annals paper from the 2020s which mentions them. So let's make an automorphic representation challenge!

Hmm, OK, well an automorphic reprsesentation is a representation of the adelic points of a connected reductive group over a global field which appears as a subquotient of a space of automorphic forms. Hmm, so we need to define "reductive group over a field" and "automorphic form". This is a bifurcation.

Let's go down the first route. We need to define "reductive group over a field". It's worth stressing that a reductive group is not a group. What is it exactly? Well, it's either a group variety, or a Hopf algebra, or a group functor. Wait -- so we don't even know the type of this definition! There are three distinct choices here. Someone is going to have to make a decision here. If the idea is to get this definition into mathlib then there needs to be a discussion. Then we need to pick up the pieces -- we need to define "connected reductive", "global field" etc (although these are easier)

Now let's try the second path. We need to define "automorphic form". For that we need to talk about C^infty functions on the real points of a connected reductive group. So we haven't even decided what the type of "connected reductive group" is, but whatever we choose, it will certainly be the case that if we take the connected reductive group E8E_8E8​ over Q\mathbb{Q}Q and then take its real points, this will be a group, but it's not going to be a real manifold. So now we have to make it into a real manifold. This is a very delicate construction, which probably needs something like the implicit function theorem (which I don't think we have) and also arguments saying that a connected reductive group is nonsingular (a theorem in algebraic geometry) and hence the real points are smooth (another result in analysis). Probably the correct thing to do here as far as mathlib is concerned is to let kkk be a nontrivially normed field and let XXX be a smooth algebraic variety over kkk, and then give X(k)X(k)X(k) a manifold structure, which is far more general but which is probably the correct thing to do. And then you also need that if kkk is a field and if RRR is a topological kkk-algebra then the RRR-points of a kkk-variety have a canonical topology (which maybe we have by now?). And then you will need the action of the Lie algebra of a Lie group on the C∞C^\inftyC∞ functions on the group (via first order differential operators), which again we might be close to having or even have.

So this one naive goal ("state the global Langlands conjectures") throws out subgoal after subgoal until it actually looks like a nontrivial research project to even write the automorphic form challenge. A possible way to start is simply to go right down to the bottom and ask questions such as "how is mathlib going to define the concept of an algebraic group", but certainly AI is not going to help with that.

I think these are problems that can be tackled from a software engineering standpoint. Let me use first-order logic and model theory to help illustrate.

Suppose I develop my theory (let us call it a textbook) on doohickeys and their potential for excellence. If I am to teach this subject, I not only describe many/all of the properties as a schema of statements (I like FOL but more expressive logics/languages can be considered), AND I also provide a list of models (call them examples) of things which satisfy these properties and some which don't. Even if I don't have a complete list of examples (a classification theorem) to help me define doohickeys, I have a start on the theory by considering Th(S \dotcup T), the collection of first order statements phi such that any example in S satisfies all such phi, and such that there is a model in T and a statement phi from this theory such that the model satisfies not phi. (More concretely, there is a proof from a fragment of the theory that T is a structure which is not a model of the theory. ) So my textbook has statements and example structures, some of which are models of the theory and some which are not (with demonstrations establishing each kind).

Now I have my set of statements and examples from my textbook "The Excellence of Doohickeys", and I ask Claustotle (my new proprietary AI agent) to autoformalize my textbook. It produces a set of statements, and a set of examples, and its output mirrors the structure of my textbook, but I can't glance at the output and conclude whether anything has been misformalized.

What I can do is investigate the pattern of examples and structures. If Claustotle has changed the shape of the structures used to express the theory, that should be a warning to me. However, suppose I find a way to translate my list into a parallel list following the AI output. (I assume also that for each example E , I have the ability to show that trans(E) is either isomorphic to or elementarily equivalent to E , in short I can quickly test the AI representation of the structure trans(E) ) I can now use my translation of my examples to work through the AI textbook and see that my idea of the structure fits the AI's idea of the theory.

In software engineering, this is called test cases or a test suite. I may not be able to capture all the differences between all the ramifications of my text and those from the AI text, but if I see no differences in my example set and the translated version, I can build confidence in the AI text and enhance it by verifying all examples against all statements. In particular, if I have a quasi-excellent special doohicky which is not excellent, I have increased my understanding of the set of models of my theory and come up with a test case for future revisions of the test book.

These test-cases change the mind-reading problem into the "software specification and requirement" problem: It doesn't matter if I can read the mind of my client as long as I and the client agree on what the example set is supposed to be and what some of the target sentences (theorems? conjectures?) are supposed to be to measure behaviour.

The iceberg problem can be seen as a need to generate more test cases which may/may not meet certain standards. If only we had a technology to suggest to us things to try...

Again, one can certainly go down this road, but the point is that it runs counter to the philosophy of many people in the formal methods community. As an analogy, suppose we ask the question, how do I know that my code is bug-free? One answer is, "Well, I did a bunch of tests and everything passed." But fans of formal methods typically aren't happy with that answer. They want to have a formal spec and a formal proof that the code matches the spec. If you now say, "I don't have a formal spec but here are some notes that I scribbled down from the standards meeting, so let's just let AI read those notes and craft a formal spec," you can see why people might feel queasy.

To be clear, I'm not saying that we can't do some things to prevent an autoformalized definition from being way off. My offhand comment earlier about error-correcting codes and probabilistically checkable proofs was made with this sort of thing in mind. Rather, my main point is that if we just decide to trust AI to solve the Mind-Reading Problem, then we're definitely sacrificing something. It's qualitatively different from trusting AI to autonomously fill in a sorry for a formal theorem that we are totally sure expresses what we intend. Now maybe we're willing to make that sacrifice, because we live in an imperfect world. Fine. Having a clear idea of what one is sacrificing, and consciously sacrificing it anyway, is a judgment call. What I'm concerned about is that some people don't seem to realize that something is being sacrificed when we trust AI to autonomously solve the Mind-Reading Problem.

Then it is incumbent upon us to discuss, reveal, simplify, and explain the issues involved. I think you (Timothy) have been doing good work in this area, and appreciate your efforts so far. I think that the Mind-Reading and Iceberg phrasings are useful, but still need tweaking. I think the "software requirement" scenario is relevant and applicable, and hope that you can mix that into the framework you are building.

(Further, I am never suggesting that humans fully trust AI output. If the humans want to surrender the grunt-work to AIs, so be it. If they also want to surrender their understanding and capacity for creation and questioning too, then all is lost.)

import Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.Basic
import Mathlib.Geometry.Manifold.VectorBundle.SmoothSection
import Mathlib.Geometry.Manifold.VectorBundle.Tangent
import Mathlib.Topology.VectorBundle.Hom
/-!
# Genus of a compact Riemann surface

Defined as the ℂ-dimension of global holomorphic 1-forms:
`genus X := Module.finrank ℂ (HolomorphicOneForms X)`.

This matches the analytic definition; with real content
(`FiniteDimensional ℂ (HOF X)` from Cartan–Serre) it agrees with the
topological definition `finrank ℤ (H₁(X, ℤ)) / 2` by Riemann–Roch /
Dolbeault.

The `HolomorphicOneForms` definition is inlined here (rather than
imported from `HolomorphicForms.lean`) to avoid a circular dependency:
`HolomorphicForms.lean` imports `Genus.lean`.
-/

namespace Jacobians

open scoped Manifold ContDiff Bundle

/-- The ℂ-vector space of global analytic sections of the cotangent bundle
of a compact connected complex 1-manifold.

Mathematically: global holomorphic 1-forms on `X`. Defined here (rather
than in `HolomorphicForms.lean`) so that `genus` below can refer to it. -/
def HolomorphicOneForms (X : Type*) [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X] [CompactSpace X]
    [ConnectedSpace X] [ChartedSpace ℂ X] [IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ) ω X] : Type _ :=
  ContMDiffSection 𝓘(ℂ) (ℂ →L[ℂ] ℂ) ω
    (fun x : X => TangentSpace 𝓘(ℂ) x →L[ℂ] (Bundle.Trivial X ℂ) x)

section HOFInstances

variable {X : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X] [CompactSpace X]
    [ConnectedSpace X] [ChartedSpace ℂ X] [IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ) ω X]

noncomputable instance : AddCommGroup (HolomorphicOneForms X) :=
  inferInstanceAs (AddCommGroup
    (ContMDiffSection 𝓘(ℂ) (ℂ →L[ℂ] ℂ) ω
      (fun x : X => TangentSpace 𝓘(ℂ) x →L[ℂ] (Bundle.Trivial X ℂ) x)))

noncomputable instance : Module ℂ (HolomorphicOneForms X) :=
  inferInstanceAs (Module ℂ
    (ContMDiffSection 𝓘(ℂ) (ℂ →L[ℂ] ℂ) ω
      (fun x : X => TangentSpace 𝓘(ℂ) x →L[ℂ] (Bundle.Trivial X ℂ) x)))

end HOFInstances

end Jacobians

open scoped Manifold ContDiff

/-- The genus of a compact Riemann surface, defined as the ℂ-dimension of
global holomorphic 1-forms. Since `Module.finrank` returns `0` for
non-finite-dimensional modules, this is well-defined unconditionally;
the `FiniteDimensional ℂ (HolomorphicOneForms X)` instance (in
`HolomorphicForms.lean`, content-gated) is required for `genus` to be
the "right" number. -/
noncomputable def genus (X : Type*) [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X] [CompactSpace X]
  [ConnectedSpace X] [ChartedSpace ℂ X] [IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ) ω X] : ℕ :=
  Module.finrank ℂ (Jacobians.HolomorphicOneForms X)

-- The challenge theorem `genus_eq_zero_iff_homeo` (genus 0 ⟺ `X ≃ₜ S²`) is declared in
-- `Jacobians/ProperDegree/DegreeOneSphere.lean` (root namespace, like `genus`), NOT here: its forward direction
-- needs the degree-one theory, which lives downstream of `Genus` (via `ProjectiveLine → Genus`).
-- Declaring it there breaks the import cycle an in-`Genus` proof would create. `Nonempty X` comes
-- free from `[ConnectedSpace X]`, so the spec signature is unchanged.
